title_original: “Reaching Out”: The Iconic War Photo Turns 60
excerpt_original: Life magazine photographer Larry Burrows made "Reaching Out" in October of 1966. He died in combat five years later, before the picture had ever been seen publicly. On the photo’s 60th anniversary, Blind presents an exclusive interview with Burrows’s son about why it was…

blocks.text: Mutter’s Ridge may not have the same name recognition as the Hanoi Hilton, Hamburger Hill, or the Mekong Delta, but it was the site of a series of harrowing, high-casualty battles during the Vietnam War. It was also where one of the defining photographs of that war (and one of the most iconic images from any war) was made. It was on Mutter’s Ridge, 60 years ago, on October 5, 1966, atop a scarred and mud-soaked mountain on the southern edge of the demilitarized zone, that 40-year-old Larry Burrows, one of Life magazine’s finest photographers, made a picture so beautiful, so horrible, so emotionally riveting that it resides in the Museum of Modern Art as well as the Victoria and Albert. And, as perhaps the truest sign of its place in the cultural canon, the image has acquired a name: “Reaching Out.” Even now, in this age of surgical drone strikes captured on live video, Burrows’s photograph retains the power to remind us of war’s tender bonds and brutal consequences.

Burrows was the first photographer to comprehensively cover a war in color, and after making “Reaching Out,” he famously continued to photograph the war in Vietnam for Life . But on February 10, 1971, the helicopter he was riding in along with four other photographers, was shot down over Laos. Burrows was missing and presumed dead. His son, Russell Burrows, was just 22 at the time; now 78, he has been overseeing his father’s archive for the last 55 years. (I came to know Russell when I worked alongside his wife, Bobbi Baker Burrows, who served as a photo editor at Life for more than 50 years.) From his home in Massachusetts, Russell spoke to me about the enduring legacy of “Reaching Out.”

blocks.alt: On a muddy, shell-torn hilltop, a wounded Marine with a bloodied head bandage reaches toward an injured Marine lying in the mud while other Marines hold him back
blocks.caption: Reaching Out, Mutter’s Ridge, South Vietnam, October 5, 1966 © Larry Burrows Collection

blocks.text: Why was your father on Mutter’s Ridge on October 5, 1966?

He’d been covering the war for Life since 1962. Toward the end of September, he had joined a battalion that was very close to the demilitarized zone. The idea behind Operation Prairie, as it was called, was to cut off the flow of North Vietnamese troops from the North. It was a months-long operation, and a days-long battle over a couple of hilltops. It became a very high casualty week for the Americans, but the Marines finally took one hill and then the other. One of the sad ironies is that a few days after winning the hills, the Marines abandoned them. They walked away.
What’s happening in the picture?

The commanding officer, a young, well-educated man named J. J. Carroll, had called in tank strikes but there was confusion about the coordinates and the shells hit his own position, which was close to where my father was. That’s the other sad irony: Carroll was killed by a strike he’d called in. That’s not something that was hidden, but it never came out in the early years. It was only later I learned that friendly fire set this whole thing in motion.
Is that Carroll in the lower right corner?

No, Carroll is out of the frame along with the radio operator he was with when they were killed. I’ve never found out who that man was. There have been many claimants over the years, you know, That was my father or That was my boyfriend . It’s a little like the sailor and nurse in [Alfred] Eisenstaedt’s picture of V-J Day in Times Square. The only person in the picture I can swear by is Jeremiah Purdie, and Purdie didn’t know who that Marine was, either.
Tell me about Purdie.

He’s the Marine in the middle of the frame with the bloody bandage. Jeremiah Purdie had signed up for the Marines in 1948. At that time, as a Black man, he wasn’t allowed to fight; he was polishing boots and the like. So for him, Carroll, his commanding officer, was everything.

What’s interesting about this picture (and what I find interesting about so many pictures) is that what appears to be going on is not actually what’s going on. Here, we assume that Purdie is reaching toward his fallen comrade…

He may have had a natural instinct to want to help him, but all those other hands are really more to do with Purdie trying to rush to Carroll’s aid, and the other Marines are holding him back. Purdie is actually not reaching out to the guy on the ground, who he did not know, but to his commanding officer, who’s just been killed.
Looking at the image from a visual standpoint (composition, color, lighting), what do you think makes this such a successful picture?

Susan Moeller, who wrote the book Shooting War , described the picture as being like a compressed piece of movie film or video. I’ve always liked that suggestion. You can imagine what happened before and afterward. It’s a very well-framed picture, but things are happening outside of it that you can imagine, not only at that moment but also what precedes it and what follows it.

Let’s talk about the framing. Looking at the picture, there’s obviously Purdie’s outstretched arms, and the arm reaching to hold him back, then there’s the wounded man’s left arm stretching to the corner of the frame, but there are also tree branches coming from the side: all these lines leading our eye to the center of the frame.
And in the center is the white bandage stained red with blood.
Your father was the first photographer to comprehensively cover a war in color and, to me, the red bandage feels like the beating heart of the picture. But talk about the color palette in general.

That palette is not an accident. It’s a signature. In Vietnam, my father tended to shoot Ektachrome and underexpose it a little bit, which gave it that palette. For my father, that captured the colors of Vietnam, captured them accurately. He was doing something that would seem to distort the color, but in actual fact, it got it right. People who hadn’t been to Vietnam never understood that the color of the soil is actually reddish. It was one of the things I found when we printed pictures over the years in a lab: The printers often had a desire to make the soil brown.

blocks.alt: A young sergeant with dust on his face, in a worn helmet and flak jacket, looks into the camera as soldiers stand blurred behind him
blocks.caption: © Larry Burrows Collection

blocks.text: The scene itself is violent, chaotic, desperate…
There’s exhaustion. And a nightmarish quality. The landscape and the people have been through hell. But for all of that, there’s a beauty to the image.
It’s a beautiful picture of an ugly moment.
And as a result, you’ve continued to look at it.
Beauty aside, what do you think makes it an iconic photo? Sixty years later, what still makes “Reaching Out” hit so hard?

There are better-known pictures. You can talk about Eddie Adams [“Saigon Execution”], Malcolm Browne [the burning monk], and Kim Phúc [known as the “Napalm Girl”], each of which won a Pulitzer. Those would get anybody’s attention in any time period because of what’s going on in the picture. But I don’t think they tell anything like the story that “Reaching Out” tells. Those pictures are memorable because they focus on single individuals and the message is very clear cut. I think my father’s picture is, by comparison, ambiguous, and it takes in all of Vietnam. It’s the American experience in Vietnam in one frame.
Say more about that.

It’s a picture full of humanity. It’s showing real-life people in the midst of a horrible situation. And it has the colors that are distinctly associated with Vietnam. We’ve all seen photos from WWII and the liberation of France: A jeep with a white American star on the hood in a quaint French village. You know immediately what it is. In the same way (and I’m not exactly without bias here), I think this picture captures all of the Vietnam War as fought by the Americans. I’m not going to say that “Reaching Out” is the picture for the world, but from the American perspective? I think it’s as quintessential as you can get.

For me, there’s staying power to this picture in part because of what appears to be the sense of brotherhood between the Black and the white Marines (I can’t think of another iconic war photograph featuring that element) and, also, the photograph feels like a Renaissance painting. I mean, the Marine on the ground is almost Christ-like.

I’d like to think my father brought a history to this moment. His early days as a photographer for Life were spent in European museums reproducing the great paintings from their collections. So he brought a sense of composition and color and gesture to the occasion. None of that was accidental. A number of times he told me that, as a photographer, you have to run your eye around the border of the frame before you take the picture because you want to know what’s in there. Cecil Beaton once described the picture as a great oil painting. I like the comparison to a painting because a painting takes hours, days, or years. There’s something much more considered than a 60th of a second.

[Ed. Note: “With the war in Vietnam,” Beaton wrote, “Burrows achieved his apogee. Some of his pictures are contemporary versions of the grand compositions of [French painter Jean-Louis-Ernest] Meissonier. They are tableaux vivants, packed with incident and details of extraordinary horror and beauty, showing us the wounded, those about to die, and those recently dead. They are the nearest we have to a demonstration that the camera could say everything that the grandiose historical paintbrush has ever attempted.”]

blocks.alt: Four soldiers take cover behind a large clay jar and a palm trunk in a burned-out village, a wooden house on stilts behind them
blocks.caption: © Larry Burrows Collection

blocks.text: Given how strong this picture is, and how focused Americans were on the war, it’s always been a mystery to me why “Reaching Out” wasn’t published in Life soon after your father made it.

Life published a vertical variation of the picture in the October 28, 1966, issue, which was a report on the war [“ Marines Blunt the Invasion From the North “] and which was credited to my father and Co Rentmeester, another Life photographer, who was miles away at [an artillery base called] the Rockpile.

links.text: Marines Blunt the Invasion From the North

blocks.text: To your eye, does the vertical pack the same punch?

Doesn’t compare. It’s nowhere near as good. My father shot approximately 36 rolls of film on Operation Prairie and there are maybe five, six frames of this moment. Instead of running the horizontal “Reaching Out,” there’s a spread with two full-page vertical pictures taken by my father, including the one with Purdie. The vertical shows a little bit more of the hill Purdie has just come down. He’s still being steadied and helped. I find the way Life laid out the story to be choppy and awkward.

The horizontal image, the picture we know as “Reaching Out,” did not run in the magazine until February 26, 1971. It appeared as a part of a tribute to your father two weeks after his helicopter was shot down and he was presumed dead. After being ignored for so long, how did the picture surface?

Whenever my father returned to the States, the Life ad sales team would take him on the road and have him talk to potential advertisers. The idea that a few weeks earlier, he’d been in the mud in Vietnam was priceless for storytelling and sales. But he wasn’t a natural speaker, so he wanted to show pictures. He used a carousel tray that had 80 frames. I think the last time he did this would have been 1969. Anyway, “Reaching Out” was one of the pictures he had selected for the carousel.

When he’d return to Hong Kong, where he was based, he’d leave the carousel tray with Anne Drayton, who was the assistant to the director of photography. Anne kept it in the credenza behind her desk. When the news about my father reached New York, she gave the carousel to the assistant managing editor. On February 19, Life ran the news of my father’s almost certain death, and the next week, they ran a very elegant portfolio of some of my father’s Vietnam pictures. That was the first time “Reaching Out” appeared in the magazine.
How did the picture come to be called “Reaching Out”?

I believe Life used it as part of a caption in 1971, but today, in retrospect, it just seems a natural description. [ Life’s caption read, “At a first-aid center, during Operation Prairie, a wounded GI reaches out toward a stricken comrade.”]
Was there a reaction to the picture when it was published?

I don’t recall there being one, but I was in Hong Kong, and it was a murky period for me because my father had just died. But from that moment on, it became one of his most used pictures, along with a couple from Yankee Papa [Burrows’s classic Vietnam essay, “ One Ride with Yankee Papa 13 “] and it took on a life of its own.

The writer Susan Moeller, who you mentioned earlier, wrote that “Reaching Out” was published at a moment when the country’s frustration and discontent with the war had hit a high point. When the picture was eventually seen, she says, it no longer represented a news image but rather came to encapsulate the senselessness of the war itself and the country’s desperation to see it end. Would you agree with that?

I’ve never thought of it in that way, but I can see she has a point. Truly interesting. Friendly fire, for instance, was not discussed as having anything to do with the photograph until decades later, so yes, the photograph can be looked at in a different way at a different time.
Your father shot the war in Vietnam from 1962 to 1971, a long time to be in such a dangerous place. Did he ever talk to you about why?

It’s become trite and jaded to say this, but my father wanted people to understand the horrors of war. Quite genuinely, he felt it was his business to inform, and I think he felt he was doing what he should have been doing and being as honest as he could be.
Your father was known as “the compassionate photographer,” and while his pictures were both honest and hard hitting, they weren’t gory. Why didn’t he show us that side of the war?

Plenty of photographers took very bloody, gruesome pictures in Vietnam, but my father went at it with a mindset of if you have a magazine at the breakfast table with a picture of somebody with his head blown off, you know, who’s going to stick around and look at it? They’ll just turn the page quickly instead of what you want, which is for them to take it in and consider what it means.

blocks.text: Sadly, we know what happened to your father. Can you tell us what happened to Jeremiah Purdie?

My father never knew Purdie. He only learned his name belatedly, after Maynard Parker, a Life writer also in Vietnam, tracked down the information. My father apologized to his editors at Life that in this instance his captioning was not up to par; because of the sniper fire on Mutter’s Ridge, he told them, he wasn’t about to wave around a white notebook. So he didn’t get Purdie’s name.

Shortly after the picture was taken, Purdie was put on a helicopter and flown to a hospital ship, never to return to Vietnam. That was Purdie’s third wounding in Vietnam, and with that you get taken out of the country. After the war, Purdie spent a couple of years in the Marines, moved to North Carolina, and went on to become a very religious man, the deacon in his church. It can’t be overstated how important religion became to him.

I first met Purdie in the ’80s and the last time I saw him was in 2003. He died in 2005, ultimately of heart failure, I believe, but he had multiple cancers that probably were due to the filthy and polluted conditions that Black soldiers were exposed to in the segregated units at Camp Lejeune where Purdie spent his early days as a Marine. By the way, although his name was Jeremiah, or Jerry, everybody called him Gunny, because he’d been a gunnery sergeant major. Purdie’s wife, Virginia, who he called Angel, is alive and well. I still speak to her every so often.

In his home, on his mantelpiece, Purdie kept a copy of “Reaching Out” as well as some of the shrapnel that was removed from his body. While he embraced the idea of reaching out, he did not take credit for what was happening in the picture because, as he told me, he had no memory of reaching out to the Marine on the ground. We can ascribe to him a natural tendency or a gracious tendency, but he did not claim it himself. That said, he did want to help his commanding officer.
Have your feelings about the picture changed over the past 60 years?

They changed when I came to know Purdie. That was really an honor in my life. He was a remarkable man and a beloved person in his community. That’s when the words “reaching out” took on real meaning for me because they summed up the person I came to know.
What did your father think of the picture?

We never talked about it. I like to think that, if he hadn’t died and Life hadn’t done a retrospective, at some point someone would have looked back and said, Hey, here’s a picture! But it’s better knowing that he’s the one who selected that picture, slipped it into the carousel and put it on the road to recognition.

blocks.alt: Larry Burrows in a field jacket and thick-rimmed glasses, a towel around his neck and two Leica cameras on his chest
blocks.caption: Larry Burrows © Roger Mattingly

blocks.text: Do you feel your father in this photograph?

As soon as I see the picture I think of my father. But I don’t actually see him taking it. I think of him being in the picture and not in the picture at the same time, because, you know, he wanted to blend in. He certainly wouldn’t want his presence to change what was happening in any way. That was important to him. He wanted to be in the room where it happened but didn’t want to change anything. At the time, there was no such thing as embedding (no permissions or anything like that), but of course it was the ultimate embedding. He was living with the Marines but not taxing them. My father would never take a drink from a Marine’s water bottle, even if he didn’t have water. He did not want to be the photographer dropping in, taking pictures, and leaving. The thing that pleased him most was to hear somebody say, You’ve taken your chances along with the rest of us.
“Reaching Out” is in museums and books, and has become part of the culture. But what does it mean for you, on a personal level, that the picture is now deep into middle age?

I’ve actually not thought about it before. But I suppose there’s some sadness that we’re forgetting Vietnam, that it’s fading into history. Also, my father reached his pinnacle in Vietnam (everything before that was learning), and the sadness for me is that because he died at 44, he wasn’t around to take the pictures he would have taken in the decades to follow. Purdie isn’t alive. My father isn’t alive. I don’t know how many people in that picture are alive. As a friend once put it to me, the film was in his camera, and the sunlight shone off the people, and traveled through the lens, and was captured on that piece of film. It is the only witness we’ve got.
The pictures in this story appear in the book Larry Burrows: Vietnam , the quintessential and most complete look at Burrows’s Vietnam work, published by Alfred A. Knopf in 2002.
